Question 1
Type: Written
Question
أوجد قيمة التكامل التالي الذي يحتوي على جذور صماء:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msubsup><mo>∫</mo><mn>0</mn><mn>1</mn></msubsup><mfrac><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></msqrt><mi>x</mi></mfrac><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math>
Answer
Based on the reference material, the solution for the integral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∫</mo><mfrac><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></msqrt><mi>x</mi></mfrac><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math> is performed using the following steps:
1. **Substitution:** Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></msqrt></math>. This implies <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math>.
2. **Differentiation:** Differentiating both sides gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>2</mn><mi>u</mi><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math>, which simplifies to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></math>.
3. **Substitution into Integral:** The integral becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∫</mo><mfrac><mi>u</mi><mi>x</mi></mfrac><mo>⋅</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></mfrac><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi></math>.
4. **Simplification:** Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, the integral transforms to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>∫</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi></math>.
5. **Final Result (Indefinite):** After performing the integration and back-substitution for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi></math>, the result is:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>4</mn></mfrac><mi>ln</mi><mfenced open="|" close="|"><mfrac><mrow><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></msqrt><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></math>
Topic Summary
Integration involving radicals (often called "irrational" or "surd" integrals) frequently requires algebraic substitutions to transform the integrand into a rational function. A common technique is the "rationalizing substitution," where the entire radical expression is set equal to a new variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi></math>. This method is particularly effective when the derivative of the expression inside the radical can be related to other terms in the integral.

In this specific problem, the substitution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></msqrt></math> is used. This is a strategic choice because it allows us to express <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math> in terms of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi></math>. The resulting integral, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∫</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi></math>, is a rational function that can be solved using partial fraction decomposition or by rewriting the numerator as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>u</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></math>.

Key steps in solving complex integrals:
*   **Identification:** Determine if the integral contains a radical of the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msqrt><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></msqrt></math>.
*   **Substitution:** Set <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></msqrt></math> and find <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math>.
*   **Algebraic Manipulation:** Replace all instances of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math> with expressions in <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi></math>.
*   **Integration:** Solve the simplified integral (often involving <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi></math> or inverse trigonometric functions).
*   **Back-substitution:** Return to the original variable <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math>.

Question 2
Type: Written
Question
إذا كانت الدالة معرفة كالتالي، أوجد المشتقة الأولى بالنسبة لـ x:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mfenced><msqrt><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></msqrt></mfenced></math>
Answer
The derivative is found by first simplifying the function using logarithm properties:
1. **Simplification:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><msup><mfenced><mfrac><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mfenced><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mfenced open="[" close="]"><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>-</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfenced></math>.
2. **Differentiating the first term:** The derivative of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo> </mo><mi>cos</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo> </mo><mi>cot</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo></math>.
3. **Differentiating the second term:** The derivative of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></math>.
4. **Final Result:** Combining the terms and multiplying by the constant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></math>:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo> </mo><mi>cot</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo><mo>-</mo><frac><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo></mrow></mfrac></math>
Topic Summary
Logarithmic differentiation is a powerful technique used to differentiate functions that are products, quotients, or powers of other functions. By applying the natural logarithm to a function, complex operations like multiplication and division are converted into addition and subtraction, and exponents are converted into coefficients.

Key Logarithm Rules used here:
*   **Power Rule:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>a</mi><mi>b</mi></msup><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>b</mi><mo> </mo><mi>ln</mi><mo> </mo><mi>a</mi></math>. This allowed the square root (power of 1/2) to be moved to the front.
*   **Quotient Rule:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo> </mo><mi>a</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo> </mo><mi>b</mi></math>. This split the fraction into two simpler terms.

Once simplified, the Chain Rule is applied. The Chain Rule states that the derivative of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo><mo>⋅</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. For the term <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo>(</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>)</mo><mo>)</mo></math>, we have a triple chain: the outer function is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>)</mo></math>, the middle is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>sin</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>)</mo></math>, and the inner is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>. This systematic approach prevents errors in complex differentiation problems.

Question 3
Type: Written
Question
طبق قانون غاوس لإيجاد الفيض الكهربائي الكلي الناجم عن توزيع شحنة داخل كرة نصف قطرها R:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mo>∮</mo><mi>S</mi></msub><mover><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo></mover><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mover><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>s</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mfrac></math>
Answer
To find the electric field using Gauss's Law for a spherical charge distribution:
1. **Gaussian Surface:** Choose a spherical Gaussian surface of radius <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>r</mi></math> surrounding the charge.
2. **Symmetry:** Due to spherical symmetry, the electric field <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi></math> is perpendicular to the surface and its magnitude is constant at all points on the surface.
3. **Surface Integral:** The integral <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∮</mo><mi>E</mi><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi><mi>A</mi></math> becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo>⋅</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>.
4. **Final Expression:** Equating this to the enclosed charge divided by permittivity:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>c</mi><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></math>
Topic Summary
Gauss's Law is one of Maxwell's four equations and relates the distribution of electric charge to the resulting electric field. It states that the total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to the total enclosed charge divided by the vacuum permittivity (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>ε</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>).

The power of Gauss's Law lies in its application to highly symmetric systems. There are three primary types of symmetry where Gauss's Law is most useful:
*   **Spherical Symmetry:** Used for point charges, charged spheres, or spherical shells. The Gaussian surface is a sphere.
*   **Cylindrical Symmetry:** Used for infinitely long charged wires or cylinders. The Gaussian surface is a cylinder.
*   **Planar Symmetry:** Used for infinite sheets of charge. The Gaussian surface is a "pillbox" or cylinder passing through the sheet.

In the case of a sphere, the electric field vectors point radially outward (for positive charge), making them parallel to the area vector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>d</mi><mover><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> at every point. This simplifies the dot product <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mover><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo></mover><mo>⋅</mo><mi>d</mi><mover><mi>A</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi><mi>A</mi></math>. Because <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi></math> is constant over the surface, it can be pulled out of the integral, leaving only the surface area of the sphere, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>4</mn><mi>π</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>.

Question 4
Type: Written
Question
استخدم معادلة نيرنست لحساب جهد الخلية عند درجات حرارة وضغوط غير قياسية:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>E</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></mfrac><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>)</mo></math>
Answer
The Nernst equation is used to calculate the electrode potential under non-standard concentrations.
1. **Variables:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> is the gas constant, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>T</mi></math> is temperature in Kelvin, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math> is the number of electrons transferred, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>F</mi></math> is Faraday's constant, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Q</mi></math> is the reaction quotient (ratio of products to reactants).
2. **Simplified Form at 298K:** At standard room temperature (25°C or 298K), the equation is often simplified using base-10 logarithms:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>E</mi><mn>0</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>.</mo><mn>0592</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></mfrac><mi>log</mi><mo> </mo><mi>Q</mi></math>
Topic Summary
The Nernst equation provides the mathematical relationship between the cell potential of an electrochemical cell and the standard cell potential, temperature, and the activities (often approximated by concentrations) of the chemical species involved. It is fundamental in electrochemistry for understanding how batteries discharge and how sensors like pH meters work.

Key components of the equation:
*   **Standard Potential (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>E</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></math>):** The potential measured under standard conditions (1M concentration, 1 atm pressure, 298K).
*   **Reaction Quotient (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Q</mi></math>):** This term accounts for the actual concentrations. As products increase or reactants decrease, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Q</mi></math> increases, which subtracts more from <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>E</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></math>, lowering the cell potential.
*   **Temperature Dependence:** The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>T</mi></math> term shows that cell potential is sensitive to temperature changes.

In practical applications, if <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math> (standard conditions), <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>E</mi><mn>0</mn></msup></math>. If the system reaches equilibrium, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi></math> (the equilibrium constant) and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, meaning the battery is "dead" and no more work can be extracted.

Question 5
Type: Written
Question
أوجد القيمة العددية لـ x في التعبير التالي:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mo>…</mo></msqrt></msqrt></msqrt></math>
Answer
To solve for the value of an infinite radical:
1. **Identify the recursion:** Notice that the expression under the first radical is identical to the whole expression. Thus, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></msqrt></math>.
2. **Square both sides:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi></math>.
3. **Solve the quadratic equation:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Factoring gives <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>.
4. **Select the valid root:** The possible values are <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. Since a principal square root must be positive, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>.
Topic Summary
Infinite radicals (or nested radicals) are expressions where a radical contains another radical, continuing infinitely. These are often solved by recognizing the self-similar nature of the expression. If the sequence converges, we can replace the infinite tail with the variable itself, transforming a transcendental-looking problem into a simple algebraic one.

The general form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>…</mo></msqrt></msqrt></msqrt></math> leads to the quadratic <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>. Using the quadratic formula, the positive solution is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>4</mn><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac><mn>2</mn></math>. In this problem, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mn>9</mn></msqrt></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></math>.

It is important to verify convergence. For the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msqrt><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mi>a</mi><mo>+</mo><mo>…</mo></msqrt></msqrt></math>, the sequence converges for any <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></math>. These types of problems are common in competitive mathematics and serve as an introduction to recursive sequences and limits.

Question 6
Type: Written
Question
حل معادلة شرودنجر المستقلة عن الزمن لجسيم في صندوق أحادي البعد:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>ħ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>ψ</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>V</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mi>ψ</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>E</mi><mi>ψ</mi></math>
Answer
The Time-Independent Schrödinger Equation (TISE) describes the quantum state of a system.
1. **Wave Function (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ψ</mi></math>):** Describes the probability amplitude of a particle's position.
2. **Kinetic Energy Term:** The first term <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>ħ</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></mrow></mfrac><msup><mo>∇</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></math> represents the kinetic energy operator.
3. **Potential Energy Term:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>V</mi><mi>ψ</mi></math> represents the potential energy of the environment.
4. **Goal:** The objective is to find the allowed energy levels, known as **Eigenvalues** (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi></math>), and the corresponding wave functions.
Topic Summary
The Schrödinger equation is the fundamental equation of non-relativistic quantum mechanics. Unlike classical mechanics, where Newton's laws predict a precise trajectory, quantum mechanics uses the wave function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ψ</mi></math> to determine the probability of finding a particle in a certain region.

In the "Particle in a Box" model (infinite square well):
*   The potential <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>V</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></math> is zero inside the box and infinite outside.
*   This forces the wave function to be zero at the boundaries.
*   The solutions are standing waves (sine functions).
*   Energy is quantized, meaning only specific discrete energy levels are possible, given by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><mn>8</mn><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></math>.

This equation demonstrates the wave-particle duality: the particle behaves like a wave trapped in a cavity. The term <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ħ</mi></math> (h-bar) is the reduced Planck's constant, which sets the scale for quantum effects. Solving this equation for different potential energy functions <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>V</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></math> allows physicists to model atoms, molecules, and solid-state materials.

Question 7
Type: Written
Question
احسب التغير في طاقة جيبس الحرة للتفاعل التالي عند 298 كلفن:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Δ</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>Δ</mi><mi>S</mi></math>
Answer
The Gibbs Free Energy equation determines the spontaneity of a chemical reaction.
1. **Spontaneity:** If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>G</mi></math> is negative, the reaction is spontaneous.
2. **Balance:** Spontaneity depends on the balance between Enthalpy (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>H</mi></math>, heat content) and Entropy (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>S</mi></math>, disorder).
3. **Equation:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Δ</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>Δ</mi><mi>S</mi></math>.
Topic Summary
Gibbs Free Energy (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>G</mi></math>) is a thermodynamic potential that measures the maximum reversible work that may be performed by a thermodynamic system at constant temperature and pressure. It is the ultimate decider of whether a process will occur naturally without external intervention.

The relationship <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>Δ</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>T</mi><mi>Δ</mi><mi>S</mi></math> highlights two driving forces in nature:
*   **Enthalpy (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>H</mi></math>):** Systems tend toward lower energy (exothermic reactions, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>H</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></math>).
*   **Entropy (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>S</mi></math>):** Systems tend toward higher disorder (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>S</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></math>).

The temperature <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>T</mi></math> acts as a weighting factor for the entropy term. At high temperatures, the entropy term dominates. This explains why some reactions (like ice melting) are non-spontaneous at low temperatures but become spontaneous as temperature increases.
*   If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>G</mi><mo><</mo><mn>0</mn></math>: Spontaneous (Exergonic).
*   If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></math>: Non-spontaneous (Endergonic).
*   If <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>Δ</mi><mi>G</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>: The system is at equilibrium.

Question 8
Type: Written
Question
أوجد المشتقة العكسية للدالة التالية:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∫</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math>
Answer
To solve this integral, we use the Tabular Method (D-I Method) for Integration by Parts:
1. **Differentiate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> until zero:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>→</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>→</mo><mn>0</mn></math>.
2. **Integrate <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></math> repeatedly:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>→</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>→</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>9</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>→</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>27</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></math>.
3. **Combine with alternating signs:**
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>(</mo><mo>+</mo><mo>)</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>⋅</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>3</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>-</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>⋅</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>9</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>⋅</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>27</mn></mfrac><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></math>
4. **Final Result:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mfenced><mrow><mfrac><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>3</mn></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mn>9</mn></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>2</mn><mn>27</mn></mfrac></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></math>.
Topic Summary
Integration by Parts (IBP) is based on the product rule for differentiation. The formula is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∫</mo><mi>u</mi><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>u</mi><mi>v</mi><mo>-</mo><mo>∫</mo><mi>v</mi><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi><mi>u</mi></math>. Choosing which part to be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>u</mi></math> and which to be <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>d</mi><mi>v</mi></math> is often guided by the **LIATE** mnemonic (Logarithmic, Inverse Trig, Algebraic, Trigonometric, Exponential).

The **Tabular Method** (or D-I Method) is a shortcut for IBP when one of the functions is a polynomial that eventually differentiates to zero. It organizes the repeated application of the IBP formula into a table:
*   **Column D:** The polynomial to be differentiated.
*   **Column I:** The function to be integrated.
*   **Signs:** Alternating <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>+</mo></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>-</mo></math> starting with <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>+</mo></math>.

This method is significantly faster and less prone to sign errors than the standard formula, especially for higher-degree polynomials like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></math> or <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msup></math>. It is a staple technique in engineering and physics where such integrals frequently appear in Fourier series and differential equations.

Question 9

Question
عبر عن الطاقة الكلية لجسيم يتحرك بسرعة تقترب من سرعة الضوء:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msup><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></msqrt></mfrac></math>
Answer
This equation represents Einstein's relativistic energy.
1. **Rest Mass (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>):** The mass of the particle when it is at rest.
2. **Velocity (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>v</mi></math>):** As velocity increases, the denominator decreases, causing the total energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi></math> to increase exponentially.
3. **Limit:** As <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>v</mi></math> approaches the speed of light <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>c</mi></math>, the energy approaches infinity. Therefore, particles with mass can never reach the speed of light.
Topic Summary
Special Relativity, proposed by Albert Einstein, revolutionized our understanding of space, time, and energy. One of its most famous consequences is that mass and energy are interchangeable, expressed by the rest energy formula <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>.

When a particle is in motion, its total energy is given by the relativistic formula:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>γ</mi><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>
where <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>γ</mi></math> (gamma) is the Lorentz factor: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>γ</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>v</mi><mo>/</mo><mi>c</mi><msup><mo>)</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></msqrt></mfrac></math>.

Key implications:
*   **Relativistic Mass:** Some interpretations suggest mass increases with speed, though modern physics prefers to say energy increases while rest mass remains constant.
*   **Kinetic Energy:** At low speeds (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>v</mi><mo>≪</mo><mi>c</mi></math>), this formula reduces to the classical <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>m</mi><msup><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> plus the rest energy <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>m</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><msup><mi>c</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>.
*   **Cosmic Speed Limit:** Because the energy required to accelerate a massive particle to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>c</mi></math> is infinite, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>c</mi></math> is the absolute speed limit of the universe for matter.

Question 10
Type: Written
Question
احسب طاقة التنشيط ثابت معدل التفاعل:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>A</mi><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow></msup></math>
Answer
The Arrhenius equation relates the rate constant of a chemical reaction to temperature.
1. **Frequency Factor (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>A</mi></math>):** Represents the frequency of collisions and their orientation.
2. **Activation Energy (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></math>):** The minimum energy required for a reaction to occur.
3. **Temperature Effect:** Increasing the temperature <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>T</mi></math> significantly increases the rate constant <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>k</mi></math> because more molecules have enough energy to overcome the activation barrier.
Topic Summary
Chemical kinetics is the study of reaction rates. The Arrhenius equation is the most widely used model to describe how temperature affects these rates. It is based on the collision theory, which posits that for a reaction to happen, molecules must collide with sufficient energy and the correct spatial orientation.

The exponential term <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>-</mo><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></mrow></msup></math> represents the fraction of collisions that have energy greater than or equal to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></math>.
*   **High <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></math>:** The reaction is slow and very sensitive to temperature changes.
*   **Low <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></math>:** The reaction is fast and less sensitive to temperature.

In a laboratory setting, the equation is often used in its logarithmic form:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi><mo> </mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mi>R</mi></mfrac><mfenced><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>T</mi></mfrac></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>ln</mi><mo> </mo><mi>A</mi></math>
By plotting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ln</mi><mo> </mo><mi>k</mi></math> versus <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mi>T</mi></math> (an Arrhenius plot), scientists can determine the activation energy from the slope of the resulting straight line.

Question
أوجد تدرج الدالة (Gradient) التالية:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∇</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mover><mi>i</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfrac><mover><mi>j</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow></mfrac><mover><mi>k</mi><mo>^</mo></mover></math>
Answer
The gradient of a scalar function <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi></math> is a vector field.
1. **Calculation:** It is calculated by taking the partial derivative of the function with respect to each variable (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi></math>).
2. **Result:** The resulting vector points in the direction of the steepest increase of the function.
3. **Magnitude:** The magnitude of the gradient vector represents the rate of increase in that direction.
Topic Summary
The gradient is a fundamental concept in multivariable calculus and vector analysis. It generalizes the concept of a derivative to functions of multiple variables. While a standard derivative tells you the slope of a line, the gradient tells you the "slope" of a surface or a higher-dimensional manifold.

Key properties of the Gradient (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∇</mo><mi>f</mi></math>):
*   **Direction of Steepest Ascent:** If you are standing on a hill described by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>)</mo></math>, the gradient vector at your location points directly uphill.
*   **Orthogonality to Level Sets:** The gradient vector at a point is always perpendicular to the level curve (or level surface) passing through that point.
*   **Directional Derivative:** The derivative of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>f</mi></math> in any direction <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mover><mi>u</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math> is the dot product of the gradient and the unit vector <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mover><mi>u</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math>.

In physics, the gradient is used to define conservative forces. For example, the electric field is the negative gradient of the electric potential (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mover><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mo>∇</mo><mi>V</mi></math>), and the gravitational force is related to the gradient of gravitational potential.

Question 12
Type: Written
Question
احسب قيمة التكامل التالي:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∫</mo><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math>
Answer
To solve integrals of trigonometric functions with even powers:
1. **Power Reduction Identities:** Use identities like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo> </mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo> </mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></math>.
2. **Expansion:** Expand the resulting algebraic expression.
3. **Simplification:** Convert products of cosines back into sums using product-to-sum identities if necessary.
4. **Integration:** Integrate the resulting terms term-by-term. This process requires significant algebraic expansion before simple integration can be performed.
Topic Summary
Integrating powers of sine and cosine is a common task in calculus. The strategy depends on whether the powers are even or odd.
*   **Odd Powers:** If at least one power is odd, we save one factor and convert the rest using <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>, then use u-substitution.
*   **Even Powers:** If both powers are even (as in this question), we must use power-reduction identities.

For <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∫</mo><msup><mi>sin</mi><mn>4</mn></msup><mi>x</mi><mo> </mo><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>x</mi><mo> </mo><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math>, the substitution would look like:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∫</mo><msup><mfenced><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>-</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo> </mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup><mfenced><mfrac><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo> </mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></math>
This expands into a polynomial of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>cos</mi><mo> </mo><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></math>. Any remaining even powers (like <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>cos</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mn>2</mn><mi>x</mi></math>) must be reduced again using the same identities. While tedious, this method is guaranteed to reduce the integral to a form that can be integrated directly. These integrals are essential in calculating areas and volumes in polar coordinates and in signal processing (Fourier analysis).

Question
طبق معادلة برنولي لحساب فرق الضغط في أنبوب متغير المقطع:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>P</mi><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>ρ</mi><msup><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>ρ</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>constant</mtext></math>
Answer
Bernoulli's equation is a statement of the conservation of energy for flowing fluids.
1. **Static Pressure (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>P</mi></math>):** The actual pressure of the fluid.
2. **Dynamic Pressure (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mi>ρ</mi><msup><mi>v</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>):** Represents the kinetic energy per unit volume.
3. **Hydrostatic Pressure (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>ρ</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>h</mi></math>):** Represents the potential energy per unit volume due to height.
4. **Key Principle:** As the velocity of a fluid increases, its pressure decreases (and vice versa). This explains how airplane wings generate lift.
Topic Summary
Bernoulli's principle is a cornerstone of fluid dynamics. It describes the behavior of an ideal fluid (incompressible and non-viscous) in steady flow. The equation essentially states that the sum of all forms of energy in a fluid flowing along a streamline is the same at all points on that streamline.

Applications of Bernoulli's Equation:
*   **Venturi Effect:** In a constricted pipe, the fluid velocity increases, which causes the pressure to drop. This is used in carburetors and flow meters.
*   **Aerodynamics:** The shape of an airfoil causes air to move faster over the top surface than the bottom. According to Bernoulli, the pressure on top is lower, creating an upward lift force.
*   **Torricelli's Law:** Used to find the speed of efflux of a liquid from a hole in a tank.

It is important to note the limitations: the equation assumes no energy is lost to friction (viscosity) and that the flow is laminar (not turbulent). In real-world engineering, corrections are often made to account for these losses, but Bernoulli's equation remains the starting point for most hydraulic and aerodynamic calculations.

To solve this radical equation:
1. **Isolate one radical:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>.
2. **Square both sides:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>.
3. **Simplify:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>, which reduces to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>6</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>.
4. **Isolate the remaining radical:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></msqrt></math>.
5. **Square again:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>9</mn><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></math>.
6. **Final Result:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></math>.
Topic Summary
Radical equations are equations in which the variable is under a radical sign. The standard strategy for solving them is to isolate a radical and square (or raise to the appropriate power) both sides to eliminate the radical.

Crucial considerations when solving radical equations:
*   **Multiple Radicals:** If an equation has two radicals, isolate one, square both sides, and then isolate the remaining radical to square again.
*   **Extraneous Solutions:** Squaring both sides of an equation can introduce "fake" solutions that do not satisfy the original equation. For example, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn></math> becomes <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>9</mn></math>, which also has the solution <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></math>. Always check the final answer in the original equation.
*   **Domain:** The expression inside a square root must be non-negative. For this problem, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></math>. Since <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>11</mn><mo>≥</mo><mn>2</mn></math>, it is a valid candidate.

Checking <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>11</mn></math>: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msqrt><mn>11</mn><mo>+</mo><mn>5</mn></msqrt><mo>-</mo><msqrt><mn>11</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>2</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><msqrt><mn>16</mn></msqrt><mo>-</mo><msqrt><mn>9</mn></msqrt><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></math>. The solution is correct.

Question

Answer
The Laplace transform converts a function of time <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>t</mi></math> into a function of complex frequency <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>s</mi></math>.
1. **Basic Transform:** The transform of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>a</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>.
2. **Multiplication by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math>:** Multiplying a function by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math> in the time domain corresponds to differentiating the transform <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math> times in the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>s</mi></math>-domain.
3. **Application:** This specific transform is vital for solving linear differential equations with constant coefficients, especially in electrical circuit analysis.
Topic Summary
The Laplace Transform is an integral transform that is widely used in engineering and physics to simplify the analysis of linear time-invariant systems. By transforming differential equations into algebraic equations, it makes them much easier to solve.

Key properties of Laplace Transforms:
*   **Linearity:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi><mo>{</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>}</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>{</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>}</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mi>L</mi><mo>{</mo><mi>g</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>}</mo></math>.
*   **Frequency Shifting:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi><mo>{</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>}</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>)</mo></math>. This is exactly what is seen in the question: the transform of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>t</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></math> is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>!</mo></mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mfrac></math>, and the <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msup></math> term shifts <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>s</mi></math> to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>s</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>a</mi></math>.
*   **Differentiation:** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>L</mi><mo>{</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>}</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>s</mi><mi>F</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>-</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>)</mo></math>. This property allows us to solve initial value problems directly.

In control theory, the Laplace transform is used to define the **Transfer Function** of a system, which describes the relationship between input and output in the frequency domain. This allows engineers to predict system stability and response without solving complex time-domain equations.

استخدم معادلة هيندرسون-هاسلبالخ لحساب الرقم الهيدروجيني لمحلول منظم:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>p</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>log</mi><mfenced><mfrac><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>-</mo></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mi>H</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>]</mo></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></math>
Answer
The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is used to calculate the pH of buffer solutions.
1. **<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></math>:** The acid dissociation constant, which is a fixed property of the weak acid.
2. **Ratio:** The pH depends on the ratio of the conjugate base (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>[</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>-</mo></msup><mo>]</mo></math>) to the weak acid (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>[</mo><mi>H</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>]</mo></math>).
3. **Buffer Capacity:** This ratio determines how well the solution resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.
Topic Summary
A buffer solution is an aqueous solution consisting of a mixture of a weak acid and its conjugate base, or vice versa. Its pH changes very little when a small amount of strong acid or base is added to it. This is critical in biological systems; for example, human blood is buffered to stay around pH 7.4.

The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is derived from the equilibrium expression for a weak acid: <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>[</mo><msup><mi>H</mi><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>]</mo><mo>[</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>-</mo></msup><mo>]</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>[</mo><mi>H</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>]</mo></mrow></mfrac></math>. Taking the negative log of both sides yields the HH equation.
*   **When <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>[</mo><msup><mi>A</mi><mo>-</mo></msup><mo>]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>[</mo><mi>H</mi><mi>A</mi><mo>]</mo></math>:** The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>log</mi><mo>(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>, so <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>p</mi><mi>H</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></math>. This occurs at the half-equivalence point of a titration.
*   **Effective Range:** A buffer is most effective within <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>±</mo><mn>1</mn></math> pH unit of its <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></math>.

This equation is also used in biochemistry to determine the isoelectric point of proteins and the ionization state of amino acids at different physiological pH levels.

Answer
To find the derivative of an implicit function:
1. **Differentiate both sides with respect to x:** Remember to use the chain rule for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>y</mi></math> and the product rule for <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></math>.
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>y</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>)</mo></math>
2. **Group terms with y':** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>y</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>.
3. **Factor out y':** <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>y</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math>.
4. **Solve for y':**
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>y</mi><mo>'</mo><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>
Topic Summary
Implicit differentiation is used when a function is not defined explicitly (i.e., not in the form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo></math>). Instead, <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>y</mi></math> are mixed together in an equation. The key principle is to treat <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>y</mi></math> as a function of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>x</mi></math> and apply the chain rule whenever you differentiate a term containing <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>y</mi></math>.

The equation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></math> describes a famous curve called the **Folium of Descartes**.
*   **Chain Rule Application:** When differentiating <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msup></math>, we get <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>⋅</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>.
*   **Product Rule Application:** When differentiating <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mi>y</mi></math>, we treat it as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>(</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mo>)</mo><mo>⋅</mo><mi>y</mi></math>, giving <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>y</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>.

Implicit differentiation is essential for finding the slopes of tangents to circles, ellipses, and other conic sections, as well as for solving "related rates" problems in physics and engineering where multiple variables change with respect to time.

عبر عن قانون فاراداي في صورته التفاضلية:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∇</mo><mo>×</mo><mover><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mover><mi>B</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></math>
Answer
Faraday's Law of Induction in differential form states:
1. **Mechanism:** A time-varying magnetic field (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mover><mi>B</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math>) induces a circulating electric field (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mover><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></math>).
2. **Lenz's Law:** The negative sign indicates that the induced field opposes the change in magnetic flux that created it.
3. **Application:** This principle is the core mechanism behind electric generators, transformers, and induction motors.
Topic Summary
Faraday's Law is one of the four Maxwell's equations that form the foundation of classical electromagnetism. It describes how an electromotive force (EMF) is generated by a changing magnetic environment.

The differential form <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∇</mo><mo>×</mo><mover><mi>E</mi><mo>→</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mover><mi>B</mi><mo>→</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo>∂</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> uses the **curl** operator (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∇</mo><mo>×</mo></math>). The curl of a vector field represents its rotation or circulation. This equation tells us that if the magnetic field at a point is changing over time, the electric field at that point will have a non-zero circulation.

Key Differentiators:
*   **Integral Form:** Relates the EMF around a closed loop to the rate of change of magnetic flux through the loop.
*   **Differential Form:** Relates the fields at a specific point in space.

This law explains why moving a magnet through a coil of wire produces an electric current. It also predicts the existence of electromagnetic waves: a changing magnetic field creates a changing electric field, which in turn creates a changing magnetic field (via Ampere's Law), allowing the wave to propagate through a vacuum.

Question 19
Type: Written
Question
اختبر تقارب أو تباعد المتسلسلة التالية:
<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><munderover><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>∞</mo></munderover><mfrac><mrow><mo>(</mo><mo>-</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mo>)</mo><mi>n</mi></msup></mrow><msqrt><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></msqrt></mfrac></math>
Answer
To test the convergence of this alternating series, we use the **Leibniz Test** (Alternating Series Test):
1. **Condition 1:** The limit of the terms as <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi></math> goes to infinity must be zero. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><munder><mi>lim</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>→</mo><mo>∞</mo></mrow></munder><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></msqrt></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></math>.
2. **Condition 2:** The absolute values of the terms must be decreasing. <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></msqrt></mfrac><mo><</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></msqrt></mfrac></math>.
3. **Conclusion:** Since both conditions are met, the series converges. However, the series of absolute values (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>∑</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></msqrt></mfrac></math>) diverges by the p-series test (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>≤</mo><mn>1</mn></math>). Therefore, the series is **Conditionally Convergent**.
Topic Summary
Infinite series are sums of infinitely many terms. Determining whether such a sum approaches a finite value (converges) or grows without bound (diverges) is a central problem in calculus.

The **Alternating Series Test (Leibniz's Theorem)** is specifically for series where terms alternate in sign. It is a relatively "easy" test because it only requires the terms to decrease to zero.
*   **Absolute Convergence:** A series converges even if all terms are made positive. These series are very stable and can be rearranged without changing the sum.
*   **Conditional Convergence:** A series converges as it is, but would diverge if all terms were positive. These series are "fragile"; rearranging their terms can actually change the sum to any value (Riemann Rearrangement Theorem).

In this problem, the series is <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mn>2</mn></msqrt></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mn>3</mn></msqrt></mfrac><mo>-</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><msqrt><mn>4</mn></msqrt></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mo>…</mo></math>. Because the terms get smaller and approach zero, the "back and forth" motion of the partial sums eventually settles on a single value. The van der Waals equation improves upon the Ideal Gas Law by accounting for real-world molecular behavior.
1. **Correction for Attraction (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math>):** The term <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mfrac></math> accounts for the intermolecular forces (attraction) between gas particles, which reduces the pressure exerted on the walls.

Topic Summary
The Ideal Gas Law (<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>P</mi><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>n</mi><mi>R</mi><mi>T</mi></math>) assumes that gas molecules have no volume and exert no forces on each other. While this is a good approximation at high temperatures and low pressures, it fails under high pressure or low temperature when molecules are close together.

Johannes Diderik van der Waals proposed two corrections:
*   **The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math> constant:** Molecules actually attract each other (van der Waals forces). This attraction pulls molecules away from the container walls, making the measured pressure <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>P</mi></math> lower than the "ideal" pressure. Adding <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi><msup><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>/</mo><msup><mi>V</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></math> corrects for this.
*   **The <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi></math> constant:** Molecules are not point masses; they take up space. The "real" volume available for movement is less than the container volume <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>V</mi></math>. Subtracting <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>n</mi><mi>b</mi></math> corrects for this "excluded volume."

The values of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>a</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>b</mi></math> are specific to each gas and are determined experimentally. This equation allows chemical engineers to accurately predict the behavior of gases during industrial processes like liquefaction or high-pressure synthesis.
